title: Using AI to decide your trading entries isn’t analysis. It’s outsourcing your accountability
author: three_red_candles

replies.author: three_red_candles
replies.body: Accountable for the answer. It can’t show its real inputs, it may say something different tomorrow, and after a loss you’ve got nothing to check the trade against, so you can’t learn from it.

comments.author: QuanTradin
comments.body:
reproducible is the whole argument for me. a model's go/no-go can change between runs, a written rule can't, and only the rule can be backtested.

that's the idea Quantradin is built on, a free paper site I made: the rule gets written once, tested on past bars, and then the fixed rule trades, not the model. quantradin.com

where do you land on exits, is a stop the model moves still a rule?

replies.author: three_red_candles
replies.body:
Only if the way it moves is written down in advance. A trail of 2x ATR or “move to breakeven at 1R” is a rule, you can backtest it, and it gives the same answer every time. A stop the model decides to move in the moment is just discretion with extra steps, and you’re back to not being able to reproduce or review it.

Tightening is the easy case, loosening is where it falls apart, since that’s the move most of us rationalize after the fact. I built Krino for exactly this, applying your own written rules and risk limits before the trade and keeping a record of every decision.

replies.author: QuanTradin
replies.body: loosening is the one I'd just make impossible: the rule can tighten or exit, never widen. then there's nothing left to rationalize after the fact.

comments.author: tradematesHQ
comments.body: The reproducibility point is the whole game. If you can't write the rule down and get the same answer twice, it's not a strategy, it's a vibe. AI is fine for journaling, not for sizing.

replies.author: three_red_candles
replies.body: Absolutely. No AI can take place in decision taking cause it’s not deterministic. For me, rules are rules and that’s non negotiable. That’s how I adapted in krino

comments.author: QATSAlgo
comments.body:
I’d separate AI helping author a rule from AI choosing the live action. A generated rule can still be frozen, inspected and tested with fixed inputs; its results then belong to that specific rule version, not to whatever the model says tomorrow. Any claimed journal pattern should face an untouched validation set before it changes sizing or execution.



We’re QATS. If you want to try that distinction in a prop workflow, our AI-assisted Bot Builder exposes strategy logic as inspectable entry/exit blocks with backtesting: [https://prop.qats.us/bot-builder](https://prop.qats.us/bot-builder) . It is an optional paid add-on, not evidence of an edge. Evaluations and initial funded accounts are simulated and account risk controls still apply.

comments.author: Shoddy_Peanut7320
comments.body: I agree with the split, and I haven’t seen anyone show a clean record of AI picking the live trades over a real sample. The way I’d test the journal patterns is to find them on the older trades only, then check them on the most recent trades the model never saw, before they change any size or stop. Using AI to help write a rule is a different thing, as long as the rule is then frozen and tested the same way every time. Cymetica’s Backtest Labs is one place to test a frozen rule against history with fees included.
